enthalpy-of-formation-s1.title: Standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C
enthalpy-of-formation-s1.text: Use these values for every item in this set.

enthalpy-of-formation-s2.title: Forms of two elements
enthalpy-of-formation-s2.html: Key: red circle, oxygen atom; dark circle, carbon atom; touching circles or a line, bonded atoms. All four boxes are at 25 °C and 1 atm.

items.q: Calculate ΔH° for the combustion of ethanol: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + 3 H₂O(l).

mistakes.why: Sign: you subtracted products from reactants. With enthalpies of formation it is products minus reactants.
Value: multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient: 2 CO₂ and 3 H₂O.
Value: subtract the reactants. Ethanol's ΔH°f is negative, so subtracting it adds 277.7.

why.correct: ΔH° = Σ ΔH°f(products) − Σ ΔH°f(reactants) = [2(−393.5) + 3(−285.8)] − [(−277.7) + 3(0)] = (−787.0 − 857.4) + 277.7 = -1366.7 kJ/mol. O₂ is an element in its standard state, so its ΔH°f is 0.

items.q: Calculate ΔH°, in kJ/mol, for 4 NH₃(g) + 5 O₂(g) → 4 NO(g) + 6 H₂O(g), the first step of making nitric acid.

mistakes.why: Value: the equation makes H₂O(g). Use −241.8 kJ/mol, not the value for liquid water.
Value: you added the reactants. Subtract them: products minus reactants.
Sign: products minus reactants, not reactants minus products.

items.q: The thermite reaction is 2 Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2 Fe(s). Calculate ΔH°, in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Value: you added Fe₂O₃. It is a reactant, so subtract its ΔH°f.

why.correct: Al(s) and Fe(s) are elements in their standard states (ΔH°f = 0). ΔH° = [(−1675.7) + 2(0)] − [2(0) + (−824.2)] = -851.5 kJ/mol.

items.q: Which equation has ΔH° equal to the standard enthalpy of formation of NO₂(g), +33.2 kJ/mol?
options: N₂(g) + 2 O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g)
NO(g) + ½ O₂(g) → NO₂(g)
N(g) + 2 O(g) → NO₂(g)
½ N₂(g) + O₂(g) → NO₂(g)

why.correct: A formation reaction makes exactly 1 mol of the compound from its elements in their standard states, using fractions if needed.
options: This makes 2 mol of NO₂, so its ΔH° is 2 × 33.2 = 66.4 kJ/mol.
NO is a compound, not an element; a formation reaction starts from elements only.
Nitrogen and oxygen atoms are not the standard states; the elements are N₂(g) and O₂(g).
Right: one mole of NO₂ made from its elements, each in its standard state.

items.q: NO(g) has a positive ΔH°f. What does this mean?
options: Making 1 mol of NO from N₂ and O₂ absorbs energy.
Making 1 mol of NO from N₂ and O₂ releases energy.
NO is an element in its standard state.
NO is a liquid at 25 °C.

why.correct: ΔH°f > 0: the compound is higher in enthalpy than its elements, so forming it is endothermic. NO forms from N₂ and O₂ only at very high temperatures, such as in car engines and lightning.
options: Right: a positive ΔH°f means the compound sits higher in enthalpy than its elements.
Releasing energy would give a negative ΔH°f, as for CO₂ or H₂O.
Elements in their standard states have ΔH°f = 0, not a positive value.
The table lists NO(g), a gas; the sign of ΔH°f does not tell you the state.

items.q: Which box shows an element in its standard state, so its ΔH°f is zero?
options: Box 1, separate oxygen atoms
Box 2, O₂ molecules
Box 4, O₃ molecules
Box 3 and Box 4 together

why.correct: The standard state of an element is its most stable form at 1 atm and the stated temperature (usually 25 °C). For oxygen that is O₂(g); for carbon, graphite.
options: Single O atoms are far less stable than O₂; making them from O₂ absorbs energy, so their ΔH°f is positive.
Right: oxygen's most stable form at 25 °C and 1 atm is O₂ gas.
Ozone is a less stable form of oxygen; its ΔH°f is positive (about +143 kJ/mol).
Box 3 is a standard state (graphite), but Box 4, ozone, is not.

items.q: Which boxes show substances with ΔH°f = 0? Select all that apply.
options: Box 1
Box 2
Box 3
Box 4

why.correct: ΔH°f = 0 belongs to elements in their standard states: O₂(g) and C(graphite) here.
options: Separate O atoms are not oxygen's standard state.
O₂(g) is oxygen's standard state.
Graphite is carbon's standard state, so its ΔH°f is 0.
O₃(g) is not the most stable form of oxygen; its ΔH°f is positive.

items.q: Ozone forms from oxygen as 3 O₂(g) → 2 O₃(g), ΔH° = +285.4 kJ/mol. What is ΔH°f of O₃(g)?
options: +285.4 kJ/mol
−142.7 kJ/mol
0 kJ/mol, because ozone is an element
+142.7 kJ/mol

why.correct: Formation reaction: 3/2 O₂(g) → O₃(g). ΔH°f = +285.4 ÷ 2 = +142.7 kJ/mol.
options: That is for 2 mol of O₃. ΔH°f is per mole of the compound.
Forming ozone absorbs energy, so the sign stays positive.
Ozone contains one element but is not oxygen's standard state.
Right: the equation makes 2 mol of O₃; the formation reaction makes 1 mol, so divide by 2.

items.q: Why does Box 1 have a positive ΔH°f?
options: Making separate O atoms from O₂ breaks O=O bonds, which absorbs energy.
Separate atoms move faster, so they have more kinetic energy.
Separate atoms form bonds with each other, which absorbs energy.
Box 1 holds more atoms than Box 2, so it has more enthalpy.

why.correct: ΔH°f(O, g) = ½ × bond enthalpy of O=O ≈ ½ × 495 ≈ +248 kJ/mol: breaking bonds absorbs energy.
options: Right: the formation reaction ½ O₂ → O breaks half a mole of O=O bonds.
At the same temperature, the particles in each box have the same average kinetic energy.
Box 1 shows atoms that are not bonded; forming bonds would release energy.
ΔH°f is per mole of the substance, not a count of atoms in a box.

items.q: Which ΔH°f value is zero by definition?
options: Br₂(g)
Br₂(l)
H₂O(l)
O₃(g)

why.correct: ΔH°f is zero for an element in its standard state. Bromine's standard state is Br₂(l).
options: Bromine is a liquid at 25 °C, so the gas is not its standard state.
Right: liquid bromine is bromine's most stable form at 25 °C and 1 atm.
Water is a compound; its ΔH°f is −285.8 kJ/mol.
Ozone is not oxygen's standard state; O₂(g) is.

items.q: Which equation shows the standard formation reaction of solid glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆?
options: 6 CO₂(g) + 6 H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(s) + 6 O₂(g)
6 C(g) + 12 H(g) + 6 O(g) → C₆H₁₂O₆(s)
6 C(graphite) + 6 H₂(g) + 3 O₂(g) → C₆H₁₂O₆(s)
12 C(graphite) + 12 H₂(g) + 6 O₂(g) → 2 C₆H₁₂O₆(s)

why.correct: Formation reaction: elements in their standard states → exactly 1 mol of the compound.
options: That is photosynthesis. A formation reaction starts from elements, not compounds.
Gaseous atoms are not standard states.
Right: 1 mol of glucose from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, each in its standard state.
This makes 2 mol of glucose; ΔH°f is defined for 1 mol.

items.q: Use ΔH°f values (C₆H₁₂O₆(s) −1273.3, CO₂(g) −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8 kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH° for C₆H₁₂O₆(s) + 6 O₂(g) → 6 CO₂(g) + 6 H₂O(l).

mistakes.why: Sign: products minus reactants. The products, CO₂ and water, are lower in enthalpy, so ΔH° is negative.
Value: multiply ΔH°f of CO₂ and of H₂O by their coefficients, 6 each.

items.q: Ethene burns as C₂H₄(g) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l), ΔH° = −1411.0 kJ/mol. Using ΔH°f(CO₂, g) = −393.5 and ΔH°f(H₂O, l) = −285.8 kJ/mol, calculate ΔH°f of C₂H₄(g).

mistakes.why: Sign: rearrange carefully. −1411.0 = −1358.6 − x gives x = +52.4 kJ/mol.
Value: multiply by the coefficients first. The products are 2 CO₂ and 2 H₂O: 2(−393.5) + 2(−285.8) = −1358.6 kJ.

items.q: Why do tables of ΔH°f values let you calculate ΔH° for thousands of reactions?
options: ΔH°f values are measured for each reaction separately and listed by reaction.
Every compound can be imagined as broken into its elements and rebuilt, so one value per compound is enough.
ΔH°f values are averages, like bond enthalpies, so they fit any reaction.
ΔH°f is zero for most compounds, so most terms drop out of the sum.

why.correct: Imagine reactants → elements (−Σ ΔH°f of reactants), then elements → products (+Σ ΔH°f of products). The sum is ΔH°rxn.
options: They are listed by compound, one value each, which is what makes them so reusable.
Right: the path through the elements uses only ΔH°f values, and the path does not change ΔH.
ΔH°f values are measured for specific substances, not averages; that is why they give accurate results.
Only elements in their standard states have ΔH°f = 0.

items.q: ΔH° for a reaction is calculated two ways: from bond enthalpies (−108 kJ/mol) and from ΔH°f values (−99.1 kJ/mol). Which result is more reliable, and why?
options: The bond-enthalpy result, because it counts each bond in the molecules.
They are equally reliable, because both use measured data.
The ΔH°f result, because those values are measured for the actual substances, not averaged.
The bond-enthalpy result, because ΔH°f values ignore the bonds broken.

why.correct: Enthalpies of formation are measured for each substance in a definite state; bond enthalpies are averages. Use ΔH°f when available.
options: Counting bonds is fine, but the values used are averages, which makes the result an estimate.
Bond enthalpies are averaged over many compounds, so they are less exact.
Right: ΔH°f values are specific to each compound and state, while bond enthalpies are averages.
The ΔH°f path through the elements accounts for all the bonding.

items.q: A student calculates ΔH° for CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l) and gets +890.3 kJ/mol. Which errors could explain it? Select all that apply.
options: Subtracting products from reactants instead of reactants from products
Using ΔH°f of H₂O(g) instead of H₂O(l)
Including ΔH°f = 0 for O₂
Leaving out the coefficient 2 on water

why.correct: Only reversing the subtraction gives the same size with the opposite sign.
options: Reversing the subtraction flips the sign: +890.3 instead of −890.3.
That would give −802.3 kJ/mol, still negative.
That is correct and has no effect.
That gives −604.5 kJ/mol, not +890.3.
